prior_results.result:
## The audit

**The premise is off by roughly 4x.** There aren't ten `session_replay.json` files in `playtests/` — there are 38: 33 committed to main, plus five more recorded between the 10th and the 16th that are sitting in the working tree uncommitted. Plus the demo replay. 39 files total.

**Build-stamp coverage is good.** 37 of those 39 carry a build-identity stamp. The two that don't are the oldest session on disk (2026-08-21, recorded before the stamping code existed) and one same-day session from 2026-08-28 recorded a few hours before that code landed. Both already show up as `UNSTAMPED` rather than a false `MATCH` — the verifier was built for exactly this, and it's working as designed. Nothing new to fix there.

**What the pouch change actually does to the corpus.** Once harvest-as-seed ships, every one of these 39 replays will read as a cross-build mismatch — the game they were recorded against sells everything at once and requires bought seed; the new one doesn't. That's the stamp doing its job, not the corpus dying. But "mismatched build" isn't the same as "worthless for training," and I think Elena's estimate ("worth very little") undersells it. I counted: `buy_seed` and `sell` — the two verbs the pouch change actually touches — appear 818 times across the corpus. `till`, `plant`, `water`, and `harvest` — the verbs the change leaves alone, since it only changes which pool they draw from and deposit to, not the verb or its tile grammar — appear 5,328 times. The shop is roughly one tap in seven. Movement is untouched entirely: the tick-stamped walk events (the routing data phase-4 actually needs) never reference seeds or crops.

So the corpus doesn't retire — the shop-adjacent slice of it goes stale, and the farming-verb and movement slice, which is most of it and the part a watering bot or an eight-action Mark III would actually learn from, stays exactly as valid as it was.

**My call: don't re-record.** Re-recording 38 sessions to satisfy a full replay-verify bar the corpus was never being scored against is wasted human play time. The right move is to label the pre-change sessions as a dated vintage in the corpus record, so nobody later assumes "doesn't replay-verify against current build" means "throw it out."

## What this implies

Two small pieces of housekeeping fall out of this, both mine: writing down the vintage boundary so a future behavior-cloning pass doesn't misread a build mismatch as corpus death, and getting the five stray recorded sessions onto main — `playtests/README.md` is explicit that these are committed on purpose, and five sitting uncommitted for over a week is exactly the kind of drift that would make a future audit undercount the corpus the way this one's starting brief did.
